own_scenes.desc: Rock que usa la guitarra como un sintetizador y dibuja espacios abiertos: Slowdive, My Bloody Valentine, Seefeel y, más allá, Sigur Rós. Otro punto de arranque del post-rock.

refs.q: de Slowdive y el grueso de la corriente shoegazer a My Bloody Valentine
refs.para: …como Deep Dish o Autechre. Aunque tan decisivos para el devenir futuro fueron Cocteau Twins, entidad formada por Robin Guthrie y la sublime cantante Elizabeth Fraser que, junto al tercer pilar de la formación, Simón Raymonde, exploró nuevos horizontes para el pop en guitarras tratadas casi como ambientes anchurosos y cajas de ritmo perezosas, con la voz de Fraser elevándose como una diosa. No fue Cocteau Twins un grupo electrónico (Heaven or Las Vegas, en contraposición al fundamental Garlands, era un disco casi acústico al cien por cien), pero sí marino, metafisico: se les colocó la etiqueta de oceanic rock por dibujar espacios abiertos y sugestivos, los mismos que años después surcaron bandas de pop atípico como Talk Talk o grupos de rock que utilizaban la guitarra como un sintetizador, de Slowdive y el grueso de la corriente shoegazer a My Bloody Valentine, de las texturas de Seefeel al ambient-rock gélido de los islandeses Sigur Ros, pasando por las guitarras de Bruce Licher en Savage Republic y Scenic. En otras palabras, otro punto de arranque para el post-rock de los noventa, otra posibilidad para ver en los ochenta un momento crucial en el desarrollo de la música popular más inquieta. Efectivamente, fueron lo más de lo…

podcast.title: Box Set History
podcast.body: A box set dedicated to telling the story of Shoegaze music is noted, demonstrating the use of compilation sets to document and celebrate specific musical genres. "another that tells the story of Shugaz."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music Industry Glossary: Part 1

podcast.title: British Origins
podcast.body: Shoegaze, like early Dreampop, originated in Britain. It emerged as a related genre, essentially described as Dreampop with significantly amplified guitars.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Dreampop - A History

podcast.title: Commercial Performance vs. Impact
podcast.body: Despite the fact that "no one involved sold a lot of records or content tickets," the genre exerted a profound influence. Its music is still referenced today by many who consider it formative, indicating that its impact "is still being felt today" and "far outweighed its commercial performance." "No one involved sold a lot of records or content tickets, but the impact this music had is still being felt today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Shoegaze

podcast.title: Component of Pop Gaze
podcast.body: Shoegaze is identified as one of the two main components of the hybrid genre known as Pop Gaze, blending with Pop elements to create a new style. "This is a mixture of Pop and Shoegaze."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: Connecting Movement
podcast.body: Shoegaze emerged in the mid-1980s as a crucial, though often overlooked, movement that effectively connected the first generation of indie music (Post-punk of the early 80s) with the second generation (Grunge/Brit-pop of the early 90s). "justo en el medio, a mitad de los 80, hubo un pequeño movimiento que realmente es la que viene a conectar esas dos grandes generaciones de la música indí."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La generación perdida del Indie: SHOEGAZE

podcast.title: Context within UK Music Movements
podcast.body: Shoegaze (phonetically referred to as "su case") is mentioned as part of the broader musical landscape in the UK, existing alongside Import music and the Manchester sound in the period between the Post-Punk of the early 80s and the Britpop and more commercial music of the 90s. "Ahí en medio tenemos pues el import, tenemos el su case y una de las cosas yo creo que más movidas y que más gancho tenía a la era ese sonido Manchester."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Sonido MADCHESTER

podcast.title: Core Aesthetic and Sensory Experience
podcast.body: Shoegaze music is designed to deliver an "intense sensory experience" that focuses attention inward. It is characterized by loud, fuzzy sounds that "hit you hard in the chest and savaged your ears," creating an immersive atmosphere that promotes introspection rather than external showmanship. "The music hit you hard in the chest and savaged your ears, creating a very intense sensory experience that focused attention inward."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Shoegaze

podcast.title: Delayed Commercial Recognition
podcast.body: Although bands like My Bloody Valentine and Pixies formed around 1984-1985, the Shoegaze movement struggled with scarce record industry interest, preventing it from gaining significant momentum until almost the late 1980s, creating a 4-5 year gap of limited commercial impact. "el escaso interés discográfico que generó todo este movimiento hizo que no fuese engarando peso hasta casi finales de los 80 y estuviesen ahí como un gap de tiempo entre 4 y 5 años."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La generación perdida del Indie: SHOEGAZE

podcast.title: Disputed Relationship with Dreampop
podcast.body: There is a significant and ongoing debate among critics and music enthusiasts regarding whether shoegaze and dreampop are the same genre, two distinct genres, or two facets of a single musical movement, with no official or clear consensus. "hay mucha disputa entre el sugeis y el dreampop... al margen de interpretaciones porque no tenemos claro y no hay una uniformidad en si el sugeis y el dreampop son lo mismo o no son lo mismo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: DREAM POP y SHOEGAZE. Diferencias entre ellos.

podcast.title: Early 90s Prominence and 2010s Semi-Revival
podcast.body: Shoegaze, a "loud fuzzy sound," had its peak in the early 1990s and seemed to be largely done by the end of that decade. However, by the 2010s, a thriving underground scene emerged, leading to a "minor revival" or "semi-revival." This scene featured club nights, social media activity, and new record labels (mostly British), and saw shoegaze techniques absorbed into other genres like Black Metal (creating Blackgaze) and Emo, and a variant known as Art School Shoegaze from Japan. "A Jason Tissike was a minor revival with Shougase, the loud fuzzy sound that had its moment in the early 1990s." "By the 2010s, there was a thriving Shougase underground."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

podcast.title: Emergence and Definition
podcast.body: Shoegaze emerged as a new sound, initially unnamed, during the late 1980s and early 1990s, characterized by dense, enveloping guitars, significant use of delay and reverb. It was influenced by bands like Cocteau Twins (evocative timbre) and Jesus and Mary Chain (pop wall of sound), with A.R. Kane also being a major early influence. The genre earned its name from the press observing guitarists concentrating on their pedalboards during live performances. My Bloody Valentine's early EPs and "Isn't Anything" album were considered the unofficial starting point, and "Loveless" became its defining work. "Pese a que aún no se le conocía como tal, en esa época se hablaba mucho de ese nuevo sonido que se estaba gestando, caracterizado por guitarras densas y envolventes y mucho de ley y reverb, influenciado por bandas como Cocteau Twins y su trimpó bebocador y el muro de popularista de Jesus Admiral Chain."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El disco imposible: La historia de Loveless y My Bloody Valentine

podcast.title: Enduring Legacy and Contemporary Influence
podcast.body: Although the original shoegaze era was brief, its influence persists strongly in contemporary music. It can be heard in the production work of Alan Moulder with bands like The Smashing Pumpkins and Nine Inch Nails, and directly in the sound of groups like Silver Sun Pickups, A Place to Bury Strangers, Die of Crocodiles, Toy, Yuck, Auto-Locks, The Black Angels, Sigur Rós, M83, Mogwai, Ulrich Schnauss, The Pains of Being Pure at Heart, and Hookworms, many of whom "name check my bloody Valentine as an influence." "The shoogas legacy can be felt all over the place."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Shoegaze

podcast.title: Etymology of the Term
podcast.body: The term "shoegaze" originated from the observed stage behavior of these new bands. Unlike mainstream frontmen who performed frenetically, shoegaze musicians often looked down at their feet while playing. This was partly due to a desire for the "music to do all the talking" and, more practically, because they had to "keep their eyes on the foot pedals they were using" for their heavily treated guitar parts. "To the audience they appeared to be looking at their shoes all the time, hence the label shoegasing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Shoegaze

podcast.title: Extreme End of Dreampop
podcast.body: Shoegaze is fundamentally Dreampop taken to an extreme. The distinction between the two genres often became blurred, especially in North America where the terms were frequently used interchangeably.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Dreampop - A History

podcast.title: Failed to Ignite Masses
podcast.body: Shoegaze was a music style that "had failed to ignite the masses" in the early 1990s, leaving a musical void in Britain prior to the rise of Britpop. "Shoegays had failed to ignite the masses."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 4: Britpop

podcast.title: Female Vocal Presence
podcast.body: A notable and often "overlooked aspect of shoegaze" was its significant "sexual equality" within the scene, with approximately 50% of the featured songs utilizing female vocals. Many bands included at least one female member playing a major role in vocals, creating an "interesting balance" between the "male aggression, manifested in the noise of guitars," and "soft female vocals." "Most bands had at least one female who played a large role in the vocals, and the result was an interesting balance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Shoegaze

podcast.title: Forgotten Generation
podcast.body: Despite its importance in musical evolution, Shoegaze is often described as a "forgotten generation" that never gained significant prominence between the two larger indie titans of the early 80s and early 90s. "esa pequeña generación olvidada que nunca ha destacado demasiado entre esos dos grandes titanes de la música moderna."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La generación perdida del Indie: SHOEGAZE

podcast.title: Geographical Naming Convention
podcast.body: Some critics propose that shoegaze and dreampop are essentially the same movement but were referred to by different names based on geographical location. Shoegaze was predominantly used in the United States and the Americas, while dreampop was more common in Europe and the United Kingdom. "en Europa nunca casi nunca se usó la nomenclatura de sugeis, casi siempre se le llamó dreampop si ungeis era un nombre que se usaba mucho en los Estados Unidos y en América en general... y el dreampop era una nomenclatura que se usaba muy poco entonces hay críticos que consideran que es el mismo movimiento que en Estados Unidos y en América en general en Europa tenían como nombres distintos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: DREAM POP y SHOEGAZE. Diferencias entre ellos.

podcast.title: Grassroots Activity
podcast.body: During its early, unrecognized phase (1984-1989), the Shoegaze movement was vibrant in independent venues, garages, and through the exchange of pirated cassette tapes among university students. "no salía de los locales independientes, los garajes o las tintas de cassette que se daban en las universidades entre agente."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La generación perdida del Indie: SHOEGAZE

podcast.title: Independent Label Dominance
podcast.body: The generation associated with bands like My Bloody Valentine (often linked with "Trimpop," likely a mis-transcription for a shoegaze movement) saw its releases handled almost entirely by independent record labels. "vino el Trimpop, vino el MyBlood y Valentine, toda esa generación fue a cargo prácticamente de discográficas independientes."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Influence on The Cranberries
podcast.body: The Cranberries' musical style, particularly their guitars, sometimes recalled influences from shoegaze, alongside dream pop and My Bloody Valentine. "el subeis yo creo que se le guardaba como mucho cariño."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Recordar a THE CRANBERRIES

podcast.title: Influenced by No Wave
podcast.body: Shoegaze cannot be fully understood without grasping the No Wave movement's reinterpretation of rhythm, characterized by its reliance on noise and distortion. "No podemos entender el granch, no podemos entender el subeis, no podemos entender el trimpob, no podemos entender a my bloody Valentine, no podemos entender al rock industrial, sin entender esa manera, de entender el ritmo casi basada en el ruido y en la distorsión."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Qué es el NO WAVE. Es mucho más que música

podcast.title: Integration with Rock
podcast.body: The noisier and guitar-driven aspect of shoegaze found a better reception and integrated more into the rock scene, particularly in America. Its garage-like guitar sound, where lyrics were often unintelligible, aligned more with the rock side of the Americas. "esa parte como más ruidosas se entenían mejor en Estados Unidos... esa rama un poco más guitarra de garajera que teníamos en el que las letras no se entendían y que se iba integrando más hacia el lado del roca en lo que es toda la parte de america, no solo Estados Unidos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: DREAM POP y SHOEGAZE. Diferencias entre ellos.

podcast.title: Introspection and Community ("The Scene That Celebrates Itself")
podcast.body: In contrast to outwardly performative music, shoegaze is fundamentally about "introspection and sensory immersion." Its practitioners preferred being "the underdogs," a sentiment that led some adherents to call shoegaze "the scene that celebrates itself," suggesting a self-contained community unconcerned with external validation from the British music press. "Now, shoegase was, and he is more about introspection and sensory immersion. Its practitioners liked being the underdogs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Shoegaze

podcast.title: Legacy and Evolution
podcast.body: Shoegaze's path integrated somewhat into the evolutionary scene of rock but ultimately remained a more "reduced" or separated style. While it didn't completely die out, its influence, while present in bands like Placebo, Banshee, and The Horrors, was less widespread compared to dreampop's later integration into other genres. "la mejor de su vez se integró un poco más en todo lo que sería la estena evolutiva del rock y se quedaría como ahí un poco más separado... tenemos como una vertende de su vez que quedó como mucho más reducida aunque no terminó de morir."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: DREAM POP y SHOEGAZE. Diferencias entre ellos.

podcast.title: Lingering Presence and 21st Century Revival
podcast.body: Shoegaze never truly vanished, remaining in the margins and awaiting a significant revival. Alongside its "cousin," Dreampop, it saw a resurgence in the early 2000s, boosted by technological advancements allowing for easier bedroom production.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Dreampop - A History

podcast.title: Loud, Immersive, Textured Sound
podcast.body: Characterized by floaty, atmospheric, and highly textured sound, Shoegaze is not necessarily relaxing due to its extreme volume. Live performances were particularly immersive, drowning audiences in layers of guitars, effects, and keyboards, with pounding rhythms and bass that resonated intensely.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Dreampop - A History

podcast.title: Melody in the Mix
podcast.body: Shoegaze often features more melody than post-rock, though it is typically deeply embedded within the mix, requiring attentive listening. "Shoegaze has more melody, but it's often very deep in the mix."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What Exactly is Post Rock? Part 2

podcast.title: Musical Style
podcast.body: The sound of shoegaze built upon Dreampop, taking its focus on layered sound to an extreme. It featured dreamy, loud, droning, distorted guitars, extensive use of effects pedals, languid rhythms, and vocals mixed very low, almost "barely there." "It was sort of dreamy, but also very, very, very, very loud, droning, distorted guitars, running through all kinds of effects pedals with languid rhythms and almost barely their vocals low down in the mix."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Name Origin
podcast.body: The genre's name, "Shoegaze," originated somewhat ironically from the common behavior of bands in this movement, who were often observed looking down at their shoes while performing due to their use of pedals. "dos cogen ese nombre así un poco ironicamente de ese comportamiento."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La generación perdida del Indie: SHOEGAZE

podcast.title: Naming Convention
podcast.body: The genre was named Shoegaze because of the common habit of many performers to "avoid contact with the audience" by staring down at the floor instead of engaging with them directly. "It was called Shoegaze because of the habit of many performers to avoid contact with the audience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 7: The Other Genres

podcast.title: Origin and Characteristics
podcast.body: Shoegaze was a "loud, fuzzy, buzzy form of guitar rock" that originated from the Thames River Valley outside of London in the very late 80s and early 90s, characterized by heavy distortion, feedback, vocals buried in the mix, and a "disarming amount of melody," making it immersive, semi-psychedelic, and dreamy. "Let's start with Shoegaze. This was a loud, fuzzy, buzzy form of guitar rock that came out of the Thames River Valley outside of London in the very late 80s and early 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 7: The Other Genres

podcast.title: Origin of the Term
podcast.body: Shoegaze was a genre characterized by its very loud, droning, distorted guitars, extensive use of effects pedals, languid rhythms, and barely audible vocals. The name "shoegaze" originated from British music journalists, particularly from _Sounds_ magazine after a review of a Moose show, who observed bands staring at their shoes (and pedals) instead of interacting with the audience. "This sound became known as shoegas, because the British music press noted that these bands didn't really connect with the audience much well performing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Origins and Spread
podcast.body: Shoegaze emerged in Scotland in the 1980s, then expanded southward to the Thames Valley, eastward to Ireland, and by the 1990s, it had reached audiences worldwide. It is characterized as a distinct branch of the Alt Rock family tree, rooted in the experimental tendencies of post-punk. "It's called Shoegaze, a sound that began in Scotland in the 1980s, migrated south to the Thames Valley over to Ireland and by the 1990s around the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Shoegaze

podcast.title: Overlap with Post-Rock
podcast.body: Shoegaze bands have explored post-rock elements, both genres offering immersive sound experiences where listeners can get lost in effects and distortion. However, some post-rock can be clean and clear, contrasting with shoegaze's typical wall of sound. "Shoegaze bands have played with post-rock. Both are immersive sound experiences. You get lost in the effects in the distortion, but some post-rock is clean and clear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What Exactly is Post Rock? Part 2

podcast.title: Part of Alt Rock Umbrella
podcast.body: Shoegaze was one of the "new fresh, strange and fascinating sounds" discovered under the umbrella of Alternative Rock in the 1990s. "Things like Goth, Industrial, Shoegays, Lofi, even singer songwriters that didn't fit the mainstream's view of Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 6: The Punk Revival

podcast.title: Peak Era and Decline
podcast.body: The "original shoegaze era" was relatively short-lived, primarily spanning "late 1989 through to late 1992," a "narrow gap between Madchester and Britpop." During much of this period, it was overshadowed by established Manchester bands. It fell out of favor when Britpop emerged, as the British music press diverted its attention first to American Grunge and then to Britpop, effectively leaving shoegaze "to rot." "The best years for the original shoegase era were the early 1990s, that narrow gap between Madchester and Britpop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Shoegaze

podcast.title: Pioneering Figures
podcast.body: Alan Moulder is credited as one of the "fathers" of the shoegaze sound, underscoring his foundational role in its development and characteristic guitar-heavy, romantic sonic aesthetic. "uno de los padres del sonido de Shoegays."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Queens of The Stone Age  - Villains (información y reseña)

podcast.title: Post-90s Continuation
podcast.body: Although considered "born almost dead" in the late 1980s due to lack of immediate recognition, the Shoegaze movement continued as an independent strand, separate from the major 1990s movements like Grunge and Brit-pop, almost until the mid-1990s, with bands like Slowdive, Yo La Tengo, and Spiritualized. "El movimiento Shugheiz, aunque ya nació prácticamente muerto, a finales de los 80, sí que continuaría como una especie de estela independiente de todos esos grandes movimientos de los 90 hasta casi mitad de los 90."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La generación perdida del Indie: SHOEGAZE

podcast.title: Reliance on Fuzz and Feedback
podcast.body: The shoegaze genre is fundamentally built upon and cannot exist without extensive use of fuzz, feedback, and distortion. Bands like My Bloody Valentine pushed these sonic elements to new extremes, creating the "wall of fuzz and feedback" that became a hallmark of the genre. "Their wall of fuzz and feedback and distortion took things to new levels, creating the foundations of shoegase, a genre that could not exist without these sounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Distortion and Feedback

podcast.title: Resurgence with Home Recording Gear
podcast.body: The shoegaze genre experienced a resurgence, partly attributed to the accessibility of cheap and powerful home recording equipment. This technological shift provided artists with the means to experiment and create the characteristic layered, textured sounds of shoegaze without the prohibitive costs of traditional studio time. "More low-fi, something called Bedroom Pop, a resurgence in sounds like shoegays, new flavors of hip hop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 5: (60-51)

podcast.title: Retreat Due to Grunge
podcast.body: Shoegaze "retreated into the background" without ever truly disappearing, largely due to Grunge's dominance, which "pushed Shoegaze out of the way" and threatened to overwhelm the UK domestic rock scene in the early 90s. "Instead, it retreated into the background without ever really going away. Its influences can still be felt today and later bands like Silver Sun pickups."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 7: The Other Genres

podcast.title: Revival in the Mid-2010s
podcast.body: Shoegaze experienced a revival around the mid-2010s, returning to fashion alongside punk, emo, and psychedelic music. "About a decade later, there was another revival. Straight ahead, punk came back into fashion as did emo, shoegays, and various flavors of psychedelic music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: Scottish Scene (Late 1980s)
podcast.body: Scotland was a significant contributor to the shoegaze movement and other similar sounds in the late 1980s, producing influential bands like Cocteau Twins and The Jesus and Mary Chain. This entire artistic current was often referred to as "the sound of Scotland."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: BLUR: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: Shoegaze's Failure to Ignite Masses
podcast.body: Shoegaze music "failed to ignite the masses" in the early 1990s, contributing to a lack of homegrown British material and allowing American alt-rock to dominate. "Shougays failed to ignite the masses."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Sonic Characteristics
podcast.body: The shoegaze genre is characterized by a distinctive guitar-heavy, romantic sound, which Alan Moulder, through his production work, has significantly influenced and propagated. "ese sonido lo guitarrero, tan romántico que teníamos arrastrado el Shoegays."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Queens of The Stone Age  - Villains (información y reseña)

podcast.title: Sound Characteristics
podcast.body: Shoegaze is characterized by a sound heavily focused on guitar distortion, the prominent use of guitar pedals to create noise, and a dense mixing of sounds that often renders the lyrics less discernible. It incorporates strong influences from garage rock and American rock. "el sugeis tenía ese sonido como mucho más focalizado a la distorsión de guitarra hacia el ruido, de distorsión de guitarra si pedales en el cual todo el ruido se mezcla mucho más la canción era como mucho menos entendible, tenía como esas influencias muy fortes del garaje que podía ser de sonidjuz o de esa parte del roca americano."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: DREAM POP y SHOEGAZE. Diferencias entre ellos.

podcast.title: Sound Evolution from Post-punk
podcast.body: The Shoegaze movement was instrumental in evolving the Post-punk sound of bands like Joy Division by incorporating heavy, raw, echoed, and distorted guitar work from pedals, thus laying the groundwork for later Grunge music. "esa música Pospang de Joy Division me evolucionando gracias a ese pedaleo, a ese guitarrero tan duro, tan rasgado, con tantos secos, tan distorsionados."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La generación perdida del Indie: SHOEGAZE

podcast.title: Underappreciated Quality
podcast.body: The limited memory and recognition of Shoegaze bands are not due to a lack of musical quality or evolutionary significance, but rather their misfortune of existing between two massive generations and lacking crucial record label support. "no tienen tanto que ver como su escasa calidad musical, porque era musicalmente muy interesante y muy evolutivo, sino porque tuvieron por un lado la mala suerte de vivir entre esas dos grandísimas generaciones y tuvieron por otro lado la grandísima mala suerte de no contar con el apoyo discográfico."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La generación perdida del Indie: SHOEGAZE

podcast.title: Witchhouse Influence
podcast.body: Shoegaze, along with Dreampop, influenced Witchhouse, providing ethereal textures and characteristics of a "wall of sound." "y del Dreampop y el sugeys, tomó las texturas etéreas y son muro de sonido."
